# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of heart failure that develops in the final month of pregnancy or within the first five months postpartum, in the absence of another identifiable cause and without preexisting cardiac disease [1]. First formally defined by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and the Office of Rare Diseases, the diagnostic criteria require left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction (EF) typically below 45% [2]. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group later refined the definition, removing the strict requirement for LV dilatation [3]. PPCM remains a diagnosis of exclusion and an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide [4].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies substantially by geography, with rates as high as 1 in 100 deliveries in Nigeria and 1 in 300 in Haiti, compared with approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 in the United States and Europe [5,6]. Established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, preeclampsia, hypertension, and African ancestry [7,8]. A global registry coordinated by the ESC has helped characterize regional differences in presentation and outcomes [9].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but is increasingly attributed to a "two-hit" model combining systemic vascular and hormonal changes of late gestation with individual susceptibility [10]. A central mechanism involves oxidative stress and the cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment, which damages the cardiac microvasculature [11]. Impaired antioxidant defenses, such as reduced cardiac STAT3 signaling, promote this cascade [11]. Imbalances in angiogenic factors, particularly elevated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) released by the placenta, further contribute, explaining the overlap with preeclampsia [12]. Genetic factors are also significant: truncating variants in *TTN* (titin) and other cardiomyopathy genes are found in a notable proportion of patients, suggesting shared biology with dilated cardiomyopathy [13,14].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Patients typically present with symptoms of heart failure—dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema—which may be difficult to distinguish from normal late pregnancy [15]. Diagnosis relies on echocardiography demonstrating reduced LV systolic function [3]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) are elevated and aid in distinguishing PPCM from physiologic dyspnea [16]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can assist in diagnosis and prognosis but is used selectively [17]. Importantly, thromboembolic complications, including LV thrombus, are common given the hypercoagulable state of the peripartum period combined with low EF [18].

## Management

Management of PPCM largely follows standard guideline-directed heart failure therapy, with modifications for pregnancy and lactation [19]. Beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective), and after delivery, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, form the cornerstone of treatment [20]. During pregnancy, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated, and hydralazine with nitrates is substituted [19]. Diuretics relieve congestion, and anticoagulation is recommended for very low EF [18]. Bromocriptine, which blocks prolactin release, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy; a randomized study and registry data suggest improved LV recovery when added to standard care, though anticoagulation is advised concurrently [21,22]. For severe, refractory cases, mechanical circulatory support and even cardiac transplantation may be required [23]. Wearable cardioverter-defibrillators may bridge patients with very low EF during the recovery window, given high rates of functional improvement [24].

## Prognosis and Recovery

PPCM is distinguished from other cardiomyopathies by its substantial potential for myocardial recovery, with 50–70% of patients regaining normal or near-normal LV function, often within six to twelve months [25,26]. A higher baseline EF and smaller LV dimensions predict recovery, whereas a markedly depressed EF (<30%) and LV thrombus portend worse outcomes [26]. Mortality ranges from 2% in high-resource settings to over 10% in regions with limited access to care [27]. Subsequent pregnancies carry significant risk of relapse, particularly in women with incomplete recovery, and counseling regarding contraception and future pregnancy is essential [28,29]. Multidisciplinary care involving cardiologists, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists improves outcomes [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a heterogeneous disorder with distinctive hormonal and genetic underpinnings. Advances in understanding the prolactin–angiogenesis axis have introduced targeted therapies such as bromocriptine, while genetic insights link PPCM to broader cardiomyopathy spectra. Early recognition, prompt initiation of heart failure therapy, and structured follow-up are key to optimizing the generally favorable but variable prognosis. Future research should refine risk stratification, clarify the role of disease-specific therapy, and improve outcomes in high-burden regions.
